title: Vatting and marrying whisky | Craft Beer School
desc: What vatting and marrying whisky mean, how long blends rest before bottling and how a craft distillery can do it well.
teaser: Mixing casks together is the easy part. Letting them settle into one whisky is where blends are won.
standfirst: Vatting combines casks into one batch. Marrying gives that batch time to settle before bottling. Both sound simple. Both decide whether a whisky tastes whole or like a set of parts.
sections:
Vatting is the act of combining whisky from several casks into one larger vessel. Historically, a vatted malt was a mix of single malts from different distilleries. Scotch rules now call that a blended malt, but distillers still talk about vatting casks for any batch.

Marrying is the rest that follows. The combined whisky sits for a period, in a vat or in casks, before it is reduced to bottling strength and filtered. Our guide to how whisky is made shows where these steps fall.
Why a fresh vatting tastes uneven

Right after combining, a vatting can taste disjointed. One cask's sherry notes jump out, another's spirit feels hot, the wood seems to sit apart. Over weeks, the mix becomes more even. Some of this is simple: the liquid needs time to become fully uniform. Some is chemistry: small reactions between components continue. Dissolved compounds settle into a new balance.

Blenders describe the change as the whisky coming together. It is easier to taste than to measure, which is why marrying times are set by experience rather than a formula.

Temperature plays a part. A vat in a warm room settles faster than one in a cold store. In Indian conditions, that can shorten the marrying time, but it also raises evaporation from any vessel that is not sealed, so keep lids closed and record the volume before and after.

Practice varies widely. Some producers marry for a few weeks. Others, especially for premium blends, rest the vatting in large casks for several months. There is no legal minimum. The age statement on the label does not include marrying time unless it happens in oak and counts as maturation under the rules that apply.

For a craft distillery, a practical starting point is to taste the vatting weekly after combining. Keep a reference sample from day one. When the weekly sample stops changing noticeably against the previous week, the marrying is doing little more.

• Stainless steel vats: neutral, easy to clean, easy to sample. Nothing is added from the vessel.
  • Large wooden vats or tuns: some oxygen exchange, little extra wood flavour if well seasoned.
  • Refilled casks: the vatting goes back into casks, often refill casks, so the marrying also adds a little more maturation.

Stainless steel is the usual choice for small distilleries. It is the easiest to keep clean in Indian heat and humidity, where wooden vats can grow mould on their outer surfaces.

Whatever the vessel, it must be clean, dry and free of any smell from previous batches. A vat used for a peated whisky will flavour the next unpeated batch unless it is cleaned thoroughly. Rinse with hot water, drain fully and nose the empty vat before filling.

Many producers marry at or near cask strength, then reduce to bottling strength in stages afterwards. Others reduce partly before marrying so the water has time to integrate. Adding all the water in one go and bottling the next day can leave a whisky tasting thin or flat. It can also trigger haze from long-chain esters.

Reduce with clean, low-mineral water, typically demineralised or reverse osmosis water. Our guide to reducing whisky to bottling strength covers the stages and the calculation.
Records that keep the batch traceable

A vatting turns many cask records into one batch record. Note every cask ID, its volume, strength and litres of pure alcohol at the time of vatting, the vessel used, the date and the target. The batch then carries a single code through reduction, filtration and bottling. If a customer ever complains about a bottle, that code lets you trace it back to the casks.

In a bonded warehouse, transfers between casks and vats are usually recorded for excise purposes. Requirements vary by state and change, so check the current notification.

Before combining, draw a small sample from each cask and make a scaled trial vatting in a measuring cylinder in exactly the same proportions. Nose it next to the full vatting a week later. If the full batch tastes different from the trial, something went wrong: a cask was mislabelled, a volume was misread or a cask was not fully emptied. This simple check catches more errors than any spreadsheet. Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky covers how blends are built.
Keep a reference bottle from every batch

From your next vatting, fill and seal two small bottles on the day of combining and two on the day of bottling. Label them with the batch code. Taste the pair side by side whenever you want to know what marrying did. Over a few batches, those bottles will tell you the right marrying time for your whisky better than any rule.
faqs: Combining whisky from several casks into one vessel to make a single batch before reduction and bottling.
The rest a vatting is given, in a vat or casks, so the components settle together and taste even before bottling.
There is no fixed rule. Practice runs from a few weeks to several months. Taste weekly and stop when the whisky stops changing.
